speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REPORT ON CONFERENCES IN OSLO AND GENEVA
speechtext:
I thought the house might be interested if I made a short report on the two conferences which I have been attending, the first in Oslo, which as hon. members know was a meeting of the foreign ministers of NATO countries, and the second in Geneva, which was dealing with the question of Laos.
First of all I shall deal with the NATO meeting, which was held under very favourable conditions. Oslo is a lovely city, almost as nice as Vancouver, particularly at this time of year.
Probably the senior statesman of NATO is the Hon. Halvard Lange, the foreign minister of Norway. This meeting was held in his home country, and that made the atmosphere very friendly and statesmanlike. Norway, of course, is a wonderful friend of Canada, and that is true of all the Scandinavian countries, of which there are two others in the NATO organization, Denmark and Iceland. With these Nordic countries Canada has most friendly associations.
At this conference the chairman was the new secretary general of NATO, Dr. Stikker of the Netherlands. It was very difficult for him, of course, having taken over such a short time ago, but he contributed a great deal to the success of that meeting.
Certainly one of the most important discussions consisted of a review of the international situation. This was commenced by Dean Rusk, the new secretary of state of the United States. He made a very full and helpful statement concerning the situation in the world as seen by his great country.
There were various centres of interest discussed, such as Germany, and particularly Berlin, and it was generally agreed that this is the most vital area in the world today in so far as east-west tensions are concerned. Other questions which were discussed concerned the situations in Cuba, Laos and the Congo, as well as disarmament, colonialism and the United Nations, and the difficult economic positions of Greece and Turkey. These 90205-6-322
two countries, on the eastern flank of the alliance, do not have many of the advantages of the other members. Their economic condition is not nearly as good, they have special problems. They need special help.
There was also some slight discussion regarding defence questions, although the main discussions on that subject will take place at the December meeting when the Ministers of National Defence and Finance will be present as well as the foreign ministers.
Canada, of course, has been very firm in her attitude on Berlin, and more than once our Prime Minister has made it clear that we stand behind the people of West Berlin in their determination to retain their freedom. In respect of disarmament, Canada's position is very well known, and I think appreciated, by our NATO colleagues. It seems very likely that the United States and the Soviet union will commence discussions early next month aimed at working out an agreed negotiating forum. I would think that all the nations which participated in the 10-nation disarmament talks would be included in the negotiating group and, of course, our own country was one of those. Probably there will be others, we hope in the capacity of a neutral chairman and perhaps vice chairman and secretary. There is a reasonable chance that as a result of those discussions which are to take place between the United States and the Soviet union, disarmament talks proper can be resumed about August 1. It would be unwise to give any guarantees about that date, but I am very hopeful that this will be the result.
On the question of the Congo, we pointed out that Canada considers that peace-keeping activities such as our participation in the United Nations Congo operation are of great value to the other members of NATO even though they do not happen to be participating directly in that very important work. There has been some tendency to question Canada as a NATO country being a member of the United Nations committee on the Congo, and perhaps a few eyebrows have been raised about our taking a part in Laos. But we pointed out that this is a role which Canada is particularly well fitted to fill, and that those peace-keeping activities are extremely important in the over-all objective of maintaining peace which is the objective, of course, not only of the United Nations but also of

External Affairs
the NATO alliance itself. I believe the Canadian point of view is approved by the other members of NATO.
We were attacked in the United Nations from time to time regarding our actions in respect of the Congo because we happened to be a NATO country, and it would be a little bit thick if we were also to be attacked by our NATO allies on the ground that we were participating in this United Nations action. I think this question has been pretty thoroughly cleared up.
On the attitude of NATO to the United Nations, I believe there is now unanimous appreciation among all NATO countries that they must play their full part in the United Nations; that it is not good enough to sit off in a NATO alliance and not be very keen about helping out in the United Nations. Canada has never seen much sense in a hands-off attitude of that kind, and there has certainly been a distinct move in the direction of our views on this question by the other members of the alliance.
The question of colonialism is a very important one. Our position on this issue is perfectly clear because of two stands taken by our own Prime Minister. First there was the stand he took at the United Nations in his inspiring speech there last September when he pointed out that the Soviet union had a great deal of nerve to be trying to criticize the western nations on the question of colonialism while at the same time there was not the slightest move on their part to give any kind of independence to the countries which at one time were free and which are now part of the Soviet union.
The other stand was the one taken at the commonwealth prime ministers' conference. That made it clear beyond per-adventure where Canada stood with regard to nations achieving their independence, and our position on this point is very clear. Mind you, the colonial question is exceedingly difficult for some of the NATO countries, but at the same time I should point out that two of the NATO countries have taken the lead in giving independence to dependent countries, first the United Kingdom and then the republic of France. They deserve great credit for what they have done in the way of settling the question of colonialism. There is quite a long way to go yet, and I think all members of NATO realize that this problem must be faced and that the countries being held as dependencies must get their independence.
Hon. members will realize that there was very good consultation at this meeting, and I think there has also been a distinct improvement in the consultations taking place in the permanent council of NATO. Canada is very well satisfied now with the degree of and

opportunity for consultation. We brought up again the question of a heads of government meeting. Once a little further progress has been made in the long term planning for the alliance, I am hopeful that the heads of government will be brought together to approve or alter the recommendations made. I think it is very important that the heads of government should meet at the earliest time that makes sense; that is, when the necessary preliminary work has been completed.
The conference on Laos was, of course, a very different kind of conference. It did not have any head, and I have never attended a conference quite of this type. There have not been many held. There was a good deal of difficulty in commencing. In the first place, word from the international supervisory commission that a cease fire was in effect was not received until the morning of the day the conference was to open. After some deliberation, the report that a cease fire was in effect was accepted as satisfactory.
Then there was another problem as to what would be done about seating the Laotian delegates. There were three sets of delegates, one from the royal Laotian government, one from the government of Souvanna Phouma, and one from the Pathet Lao. This was really a very complicated question, and almost to the minute set for the opening there was uncertainty whether or not the conference would go on.
We thought it would not be proceeding, but just to be sure and to show that at least we were not stalling the beginning of the conference, the Canadian delegation streamed up to the headquarters of the European branch of the United Nations. Nobody else was in front of the main entrance except about 150 newspapermen and photographers, who were not quite sure either whether or not the conference was beginning.
When we talked to the senior man at the United Nations he told us that he had received a message a few minutes earlier from the British, the United Kingdom being one of the two co-chairmen, the other being the Soviet union. This was the message:
We have agreed on the simple formula that there will be no meeting this afternoon at 3 p.m. (May 12) and cannot say anything about the future.
There was, therefore, no meeting that afternoon. We had a good look at the conference room and found we were to be seated next to the Chinese. We learned other details as well about the proceedings. This question of the Laotian representation was not settled until four days later. You can imagine the consultations that took place in the intervening period.

Finally this formula was agreed upon:
The co-chairmen have agreed to seat the representations from Laos proposed by the individual governments participating in the conference.
The United States proposed the royal Laotian government and, although I do not remember exactly, I believe the Soviet union proposed the government of Prince Souvanna Phouma and I think the Chinese proposed the Pathet Lao. I am not just sure which country did that. In any event, everybody was proposed but the royal Laotian government representatives have not turned up as yet. They refused to sit on the ground that they are the official government, and they would not proceed under the circumstances.
The conference opened on Tuesday last and we heard a statement from Prince Sihanouk the head of state of Cambodia which, as you know, is a neighbour of Laos; Canada, by the way, is a member of the truce commission in that country also. I thought he made a very fine opening speech. The essence of it was that in this conference the delegations should look forward and not backward; that there was not much point in threshing old straw, and we should try to see what could be done in the future to settle the problems.
I spoke on behalf of Canada on the following day. If it is the wish of the house I would be glad to table a copy of that speech or have it printed as an appendix to Hansard, and then hon. members could see the attitude the Canadian government took. I cannot do this in so far as the NATO conference is concerned because the proceedings there are secret. In so far as the conference on Laos is concerned, it is possible to hand copies of the statement to the press.
I believe that Canada's position with regard to Laos should be, at all times, to consider problems in the light of her membership on the truce commission. This commission is going to be given great responsibilities for the working out of the Laotian problems. I think we are well advised to keep that in mind, and to talk and negotiate from the standpoint of being a member of that truce commission. This, I think, strengthens our hand a great deal in trying to get our views accepted.
The conference has two main jobs to do, in my judgment. One is to support the international truce commission which is actually in the field. As you know, Mr. Speaker, there are Canadians in Laos at the present time. This conference must see that they get what they require in order to carry out their job; it must meet their requirements from week to week. The other job is to work out a long term settlement. I think that will have to be done on the basis of the Geneva 90205-6-322J
External Affairs
agreements of 1954. We base our position on those agreements, but there will have to be some modification in them.
On Thursday I intervened again to point out the need to provide that commission with airplanes and helicopters. The situation was that as early as May 1 the chairman of the commission, in his first report to the cochairmen of the Geneva conference, the United Kingdom and the Soviet union, asked for money, airplanes and helicopters. He also reported that he would be economical; that the commission would not waste money. In their reply the co-chairmen made arrangements to provide a little money and they approved of the idea of being economical- the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) approves of that also-but they did not say one word about the airplanes and helicopters.
Therefore on Thursday afternoon I drew this to the attention of the conference and said I could not see any reason why the co-chairmen should not wire at once to the commission and ask for details of their requirements. Mr. Gromyko, the head of the Soviet delegation, did not want to move that quickly. Mind you, we had him in a comer because of the letters that had been exchanged. He simply could not get away from the terms of those letters. However, the final decision was that the British and the Russians would think it over during the night, and a special meeting of the conference was called for yesterday morning at which the conference was to hear their decision. They decided that a wire would go out, and this is the message they sent: Please inform us whether the commission has any technical requirements to facilitate the exercise of its functions in relation to the cease fire.
That was not exactly what I had asked for the day before. I had asked for recommendations from the commission with regard to the number of inspection teams there should be, and for some other details. However, I thought it best to accept this offer rather than have another long argument about it.
I spoke again yesterday morning, and everybody agreed that this wire should go out. Mind you, these people on the commission have not yet got their airplanes and helicopters, but at least the wire has gone out requesting them to ask in detail for what they require. Mr. Gromyko came over to me after the meeting had adjourned and said, "You know, if you had accepted that letter without making some remarks about it, I would have been very suspicious; would have thought that letter went too far".
That is the way we stand at the moment. I am very hopeful that the commission will be given the tools to do this very difficult job. I think there is a reasonable prospect

External Affairs
for the success of this conference in spite of all the difficulties there have been. I expect to be going back in a matter of three weeks or so.
There is great value in these contacts we make with other countries at these conferences. We have had friendly discussions with the delegation from Cambodia; they are very pleased with the work of the Canadians on the truce commission in their country. The same thing happened with regard to South Viet Nam; that nation is also very pleased with the work our Canadian commissioners have been doing in their country. We have also had very friendly discussions with Thailand, with the delegation from the royal Laotian government, and with the delegation of Prince Souvanna Phouma.
I am convinced that one of Canada's most important roles in world affairs at the present time is to follow the policy of gaining the confidence of all the newer nations. They cannot be bludgeoned into doing what we think should be done, but I think if we are friendly with them and talk with them on a man to man basis quite a bit can be done in the way of getting their support for the policies in which we believe. This has been the experience at the United Nations; most of the new countries support the plans put forward by the western countries there.
I am hoping that out of this Laotian conference will come not only a settlement which will enable this little country to be neutral and enable the Laotian people to develop their country with help from outside, given without any strings, but that in addition the conference will make more friends for Canada and will help us to play an even greater part in world affairs.
I am sorry to have taken so much time, Mr. Speaker, and I will be very glad to appear before the external affairs committee at any time that can be arranged in order that members may cross-examine me with regard to these two conferences.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure I speak for all hon. members of the house when I say we are glad to see the Secretary of State for External Affairs back in his seat. We realize that he has made a statement this morning under considerable difficulty, because I understand he arrived home at 2.30 a.m. On that account one would not expect the minister to display the same lucidity of expression which normally attends his statements in this house.
The minister has reported on two conferences, the NATO meeting and the conference dealing with the situation in Laos. The minister has not given us any great detail about the NATO conference. He has expressed the view that Canada is now satisfied with the arrangements for consultation. As this is a very important matter, we will look forward to the opportunity in the external affairs committee of getting further details from the minister, particularly in relation to the position allegedly being taken by one of the major participants in the North Atlantic treaty organization. The attitude of General de Gaulle in this regard will of course be of very great interest to us.
The minister may be assured that we in this party take a strong view along with him and support the government in any steps taken to strengthen the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. We should have welcomed from the minister some indication as to what steps are being taken in that particular. Again in that regard we shall be afforded an opportunity when we confront the minister in the external affairs committee.
While he was away the minister will, no doubt, have noted that very important developments have taken place in Canada. Undoubtedly he has followed from afar the nature and character of the visit of the President of the United States to Canada. It will be of interest to the minister to know that there was some consternation in Canada and in this house as the result of a statement reported to have been made by him concerning Canada's offer to adjudicate the difficulties between United States and one country in the Caribbean. This report prompted an interrogation in this house of the Prime Minister by the Leader of the Opposition. The Prime Minister gave the assurance that Canada, notwithstanding that report, had made no such offer to adjudicate in the difficulties which might be regarded as prevailing between Cuba on the one hand

and the United States on the other. Perhaps the minister, when he appears before the external affairs committee, can tell us about this as well.
With regard to Laos, we have noted what the minister has said. We sincerely hope his optimism is warranted. We agree fully with him that every support must be given to the international supervisory truce commission of which Canada is a member. That commission, working as it does in a difficult terrain and under difficult circumstances, must be afforded every means of security and given every opportunity to carry out an efficient operation.
The minister said nothing about the relationship of the situation in Laos to the companion problem in South Viet Nam which is now engaging the attention of certain countries, particularly the United States.
The hon. gentleman has returned from these two conferences. We have welcomed the general statement he has made. Perhaps we would not expect him to make anything more than a general statement at this time in view of the circumstances of travel and the like. It is possibly regrettable that these statements cannot be more substantial in quality. This is perhaps inherent in the very nature of international negotiations. It would, I am sure, have been of great interest to the Canadian people if they could have been told with more particularity the consequences of the two meetings which the minister attended, first in terms of what is being done to strengthen NATO during a critical stage in its development; and second, that the 14 power conference was going to take strong measures to guarantee that no undue advantage was taken of this little nation in old Indo-China and that there would not be any development which would vitally affect the integrity of Viet Nam and its 22 million people.
The minister may be assured that once he has been afforded the opportunity for rest, and the kind of contemplation that comes with rest, he will find the opposition in its treatment of him generous but possibly even more searching than its spokesman is at the moment.

My
comments will be brief, for two reasons. First, I do not think this is a proper time at which to comment at length and, second, one would need to study such a statement as has been made by the minister for external affairs before being able to comment on it lucidly and at length.
The hon. member for Essex East showed some concern for the minister's weariness. Let me say to the hon. member that I think
External Affairs
his concern is unnecessary. I marched behind the minister on the cobblestones of France for a good many months, and we used to wish he would tire out sooner. We were distinctly under the impression he was tireless. I am sure we all welcome him home and am glad to see him looking in such good health. I tell him this; that every one of us, when we met in the restaurant, sent for the papers and these were perused immediately. We looked them up to see what he had said today, and then we looked them up again tomorrow to see if what he said yesterday had been correctly reported. We followed all the reports with interest because we were concerned with the serious business he was undertaking on behalf of this country.
I was particularly interested in the report of the NATO meeting in Oslo, and I was glad to note the minister's reference to the friendly relations we have with the northern peoples. They are a stable and strongly democratic race. We are proud to be closely associated with them on friendly terms. I was interested to hear about the discussions on disarmament and the economic problems facing certain members of the NATO organization. I was particularly pleased to hear the minister say today he was hopeful that discussions would commence within the next month or so between the United States and the Soviet union on the subject of disarmament. I am sure we are all looking forward to the commencement of those discussions.
With reference to the minister's remarks on the situation in the Congo and the situation in Laos, it was a pleasure to hear of Canada's continued peace-promoting activities in these very important fields. I was interested to hear the minister mention the necessity for closer co-operation between NATO and the United Nations. I understood him to say, at least by inference, that possibly there should be more co-operation between the two organizations. We in this group look forward to the time when NATO will be merged into the United Nations and all our defence activities will be within the framework of the United Nations through an international police force.
We noted in the papers some reference to the minister's concern with respect to the attitude of Portugal toward colonialism. I do not know whether the reports were accurate or not. We must not forget that Portugal, although a member of NATO, is at present in defiance of a United Nations resolution. We trust this close association with NATO will have an effect in connection with these issues which are arising at the present time.
With regard to Laos, I was very pleased to hear the minister say that Canada should negotiate as a member of the commission,

Combines Investigation Act and in that spirit. We agree with that position entirely. Canada's record in this capacity in former occasions is good, and I am sure it will be maintained in the future.
In conclusion let me say that the minister's attitude, his approach and his general stability and character represent, I think, very much the spirit and the purpose of all Canadians in their approach to the difficult international situation we face.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order in connection with today's order paper, and the order of business under the heading of public bills and orders.
Item No. 1 shown there is second reading of Bill No. C-30, an act to amend the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. That bill was called for second reading last evening during private member's hour, and I believe it should have gone to the bottom of the order paper. In support of this contention I should like to quote Beauchesne's fourth edition, citation No. 380, which reads as follows:
380. When the bill comes up for a second reading in its proper course, one of the clerks at the table will read the order aloud, and the member in charge of the measure will then move its second reading.
I should also like to read from Beauchesne's fourth edition, citation No. 385, which reads as follows:
385. If, when the order of the day is read at the table, no motion be made for the second reading or other stage of a bill, or for its postponement, it becomes a dropped order,-
The hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) had the opportunity of moving second reading of the bill at that time, but he chose instead to raise a point of order which was entirely unrelated to the bill. I believe that he therefore made the decision to proceed with another course rather than moving second reading of his bill. For that reason I believe it should have dropped to the bottom of the order paper.
The hon. member suggested, on the point of order which he raised, that the rights of private members were involved. I suggest they are very substantially involved, because the placing of this bill at the head of the order paper prevents other hon. members' bills from coming on; and, as the session might well end, this may mean the difference between one hon. member's bill coming on for discussion and not coming on for discussion.

For that very important reason I believe that Your Honour should make a decision in this regard.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I also intended to raise this matter, and should like to add a few points which were not raised by the hon. member who has just spoken.
Last evening, just before six o'clock, Bill No. C-30 was read at the table by the clerk assistant, and is so recorded in Votes and Proceedings of the House of Commons for yesterday at page 565, and also in Hansard for yesterday at page 5083. The sponsor of the bill chose not to proceed with it. It was read, and when he was not allowed to call it six o'clock, he then dealt with a point of order, which I assume it was his right to do.
I should like to present some further references. First, standing order 19 (1) of the House of Commons reads as follows:
19. (1) Questions put by members and notices of motions, not taken up when called may (upon the request of the government) be allowed to stand and retain their precedence; otherwise they will disappear from the order paper.
In this particular instance the motion was called and read, but not taken up. I should also like to refer to Beauchesne's fourth edition, citation 87 (1) which in part reads as follows:
87. (1) When an order of the day has been read, it must thereupon be proceeded with, appointed for a future day, or discharged.
The hon. member chose not to proceed with it, and it was not appointed for a future day. Therefore, I feel it must be considered to have been discharged.
I should also like to read subsection (4) of that same citation, 87, which reads in part as follows:
87. (4) It is one of the fundamental principles of parliamentary procedure that when nothing is done respecting an order of business it is struck out and cannot make further progress until the procedure regulating its passage has been regulated by the house.
Mr. Speaker, I am prepared to admit that the hon. member for Skeena found himself in a difficult position, with five minutes to go until the end of the hour for private members' bills. But I submit that this situation has arisen in the past with regard to private members' bills and will arise again in the future. The hon. member was in that position by reason of the proceedings in the house during the private members' hour. Nevertheless there was still considerable time before six o'clock for the hon. member to have moved second reading, as an examination of Hansard will show.
I believe he was placed in a position where he either had to proceed with the order, after it had been read, or to allow it to be dropped.
House of Commons
The hon. member raised a point of order in an effort to avoid having to speak on the bill, or to propose it, and I should like to quote his own words as they appear in Hansard of April 19, 1961 at page 5083. He is reported there, after the order was called, as follows:
Mr. Speaker, before the order is proceeded with I wonder whether it might be considered to be six o'clock?
The order had definitely been called and the hon. member, in the difficult position he found himself, tried to talk it out until six o'clock. I feel, nevertheless that the order was called and he chose not to proceed with it when he had the opportunity, and it should not appear as No. 1 under public bills on today's order paper.

Yes, Mr. Speaker. I do not care now, or at any other time, to become involved in the misrepresentations which have been given to my actions by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka. I should simply like to point out that there are two incorrect things involved in the raising of this point of order. The first is that this is not the time to deal with it, as Your Honour has ruled on a number of previous occasions; points of order should be raised when that particular stage of procedure is reached which is involved, which I suggest would possibly be next Tuesday, when this matter will come up again.
Second, apart from the first point I have made, I suggest that Votes and Proceedings correctly sets out what happened. The order was read by the clerk at the table and I proposed, before the motion was put by the chair-which it was not-that it might be called six o'clock. There was some objection, and I then rose on a point of order. I proceeded on that matter, but before I had the opportunity to complete my remarks it was called six o'clock. I suggest, therefore, that the order is now in its proper place on the order paper. I am quite prepared, when the order comes up again, to continue speaking on that point of order. The motion was not put by the Chair, and the stage when it should have been put had not been reached.

subtopic: USE OF CHEQUE FORMS PRINTED IN UNITED STATES

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: USE OF CHEQUE FORMS PRINTED IN UNITED STATES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, yesterday, May 19, the hon. member for Outremont-St. Jean asked a question and the reply is as follows. For some years there has been an active program of mechanization, particularly in the prairie region, of the unemployment insurance commission. The object has been to reduce the time required for processing of claims and to eliminate duplication. In the prairie region at the present time benefit warrants are printed and tabulated by mechanical process. These machines are manufactured and installed only by Remington Rand of the United States. The particular punch cards required for these machines are also provided by Remington Rand and therefore bear the notation that they are manufactured and printed for Remington Rand in the United States. This is the explanation why these warrants are printed in the United States.

maintopic: OPPORTUNITY TO PREPARE FOR DISCUSSION OF LEGISLATION

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: OPPORTUNITY TO PREPARE FOR DISCUSSION OF LEGISLATION
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the house leader. Is he aware that last night he proposed for consideration on Monday legislation that was placed on the order paper only this morning, and does he believe that the best way to facilitate the business of the house and its proper scrutiny of legislation is by not giving members of parliament sufficient time to prepare themselves for these debates?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: OPPORTUNITY TO PREPARE FOR DISCUSSION OF LEGISLATION
speechtext: Order. The hon. member seems to be mounting an argument about the conduct of the business of the house.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: OPPORTUNITY TO PREPARE FOR DISCUSSION OF LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. The business for Monday announced last night included matters that were not even on the order paper last night. Some have appeared on the order paper today; others will not be on the order paper until Monday. Therefore I think it is proper for me to ask a question concerning the business of the house, and to inquire through the house leader whether the government thinks this is the proper way to provide members of parliament with an opportunity
Inquiries of the Ministry to scrutinize, study and consider this legislation when there is only one day to consider it, that day being Sunday.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: OPPORTUNITY TO PREPARE FOR DISCUSSION OF LEGISLATION
speechtext: I objected to the question, and I still think it is not proper, because it is really a leading question for the purpose of argument and to express an opinion as to the conduct of the business of the house. If the hon. member wishes to ask a question about the propriety within our rules of the course followed, or a factual question about the business of the house, he is quite within his rights; but I do not think it is appropriate at this time to debate the course that is being followed, which is the import of the question.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: OPPORTUNITY TO PREPARE FOR DISCUSSION OF LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to continue the point of privilege, and bring this matter to the attention of the house. I think I am within my rights under the rules to do so. The question of what the business will be for Monday, as announced by the house leader last night, is quite clear. One of the things that will be discussed on Monday is an act to amend the Canada Shipping Act. I am prepared to discuss that act on Monday. There are some of us who would like to give this subject consideration before it is introduced in the house.
What will take place on Monday is this. There will be a meeting of the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines from 9.30 until 11 o'clock, to consider the Freight Rates Reduction Act. At 11 o'clock I presume it will be the responsibility of the Minister of Transport to be in the house. I am sure that in the one and a half hours available it will not be possible to dispose of the Freight Rates Reduction Act. It seems to me, therefore, that because of the manner in which the business has been arranged by the house leader, and the business that is going to take place elsewhere on Monday, it will not be possible to give this important legislation-I take it that it is important, at least until I have seen it-the consideration it deserves. If the Freight Rates Reduction Act is under consideration in the committee while the house is sitting, then the minister and those of us who would like to be in the committee cannot be in both places at the same time.
The question which I put to the minister, therefore, is this. Does he think that situation is conducive to the orderly consideration of business here?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: OPPORTUNITY TO PREPARE FOR DISCUSSION OF LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Order; that was the question to which I objected. The hon. member is in a position to ask the house leader if, in view of the difficulties he has pointed out, a change could be made in the order of business, but not to ask that question.

Inquiries of the Ministry

maintopic: OPPORTUNITY TO PREPARE FOR DISCUSSION OF LEGISLATION

privilege, Mr. Speaker. The statement the minister has made is totally false, and he knows it.

It is really only a historical point which should not take up much time of the committee. The question is with respect to the time at which a decision was made to turn the Canadian Northern Railway into a transcontinental railway, the initiative in that regard, and the decision with regard to the building of the National Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk Pacific, which was of course actively sponsored by the Laurier government from 1903 onward.
The best information I was able to get hastily about it-and I did not spend a great deal of time in research-was that while the Canadian Northern Railway was started in 1898 or 1899 in Manitoba, and while some time early in the century the Canadian Northern Railway also acquired some existing eastern lines and began to build some more, the project for connecting the eastern and western parts of the system and for building the Canadian Northern to the Pacific was and remained a purely private venture, a matter of private enterprise if one can call it that. We know that all the railways, including the C.P.R., were assisted by various grants of one kind or another, but they were not in any sense public enterprises in that they were directly sponsored by the government.
The Canadian Northern continued all through this period to be a private railway being built entirely privately. Whether the Laurier government gave them encouragement

Supply-Transport
to go ahead, or whether they did not encourage them, I think, is a matter that will be debated for a long time to come and we certainly will not settle it in the committee this morning.
However, with regard to this project as a transcontinental project, the Canadian Northern was very much the third one and came quite a long time after the National Transcontinental was inaugurated as a transcontinental system. Indeed, an effort was made at one time by the Laurier government to get the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Railway to come to some kind of agreement so there would only be one line built in addition to the Canadian Pacific Railway.
Looking back now we can all be wise with hindsight and can see that it would have been a lot better if that had happened, because a great deal of the Canadian Northern had to be torn up after it was built. As a matter of fact I think some of the section between Edmonton and Edson was torn up before a train ever ran over it because the steel was needed for war purposes in the first world war.
I have read the remarks of my hon. friend from Laurier very carefully and I do not think he insinuated-I am sure he did not mean to insinuate-that the Borden government was responsible for this situation at all. What he said was that they found that a situation had grown up in Canada where there were three transcontinental railways and there was not really enough business for them. There never has been enough business for them, because in fact one of them was interrupted and never did become a transcontinental system.
That is all the hon. member for Laurier was seeking to say, and I do not think he was seeking to impute any blame to anybody. Certainly in any remarks I made I was not seeking to impute any blame. The only reason for bringing this matter to the attention of the committee is to emphasize the important point made by my hon. friend from Laurier, about which I think every Canadian should be really concerned at the present time; that is, that we should not let the same kind of situation grow up with the air lines.
That is what we are concerned about. We see even today that Mr. MacPherson in his report is having to suggest that very considerable sums of money be paid out of the treasury to keep the railways going during a period of transition because the users are not able to pay for the service that it is still considered necessary to have in the national interest.
This will no doubt be true with air lines as it is with railways. In some areas we may
[Mr. Pickersgill.l
want air lines which will not pay for themselves, but it may be sufficiently in the national interest to have them. However, I say we should ask ourselves very carefully whether we wish to allow a situation to arise where we have two competing national air lines, neither of which can pay for itself, and where the taxpayer is going to have to foot the bill as he has done over the years for the railways. That is the point we are trying to make on this side of the house, and that was the point my hon. friend from Laurier and the late C. D. Howe were so greatly concerned about when we were in office.
We are suggesting that the government should be equally concerned about this important national interest and about the protection of the national treasury. That is the real point. I just wanted to try to clear up the misunderstanding and indicate that these things were not introduced for any purpose other than as an analogy to try to underline and emphasize how important it is.
There is no doubt whatever-Trans-Canada Air Lines have shown this over the years- that one transcontinental air line can pay, and pay very well, to the treasury; but since the introduction of the competing service we have seen what has happened. My hon. friend from Laurier warned us about it before it started. He has drawn it to our attention ever since, and we have seen what has happened. I do not take any position as between Trans-Canada Air Lines and the C.P.A. I think they are both excellent organizations. They are both very well operated in every way. I would say they are the two best air lines on the whole continent as far as their operations are concerned, as far as their safety is concerned, and as far as all those things that go to make a good air line are concerned. I do not wish to make any comparisons between them at all. However, I do say it is our primary job in committee of supply to protect the treasury of Canada, and we should not allow a situation to arise with respect to air lines which, far from protecting the treasury of Canada, is going to make it impossible for either air line to pay and is going to force the taxpayers to subsidize the services or have some of the services scrapped. That is the point.
I hope my hon. friend from Laurier will agree that I am stating the position accurately. He knows so much more about this matter than I do, and I hope he will agree that I am accurately stating the position he took yesterday.

Mr. Chairman, I have only a few words to say on this matter. I have no desire to enter into a controversy. As a matter of fact I accept almost every word the hon. member has said about the back history of the railways. There are one or two points with which I might deal, but I do not think it is necessary for me to take up much time of the committee. I wish to explain why I suddenly found myself on my feet yesterday, almost without knowing it. I am reading now from page 5067 of Hansard in the midst of a speech by the hon. member for Laurier. He said:
I am rising chiefly to point out that under the former administration we were determined to prevent from arising a situation such as that which arose under the Borden government with railways when too many transcontinental lines were built and none of them could pay.
Maybe I took it too seriously, but I felt this was leaving the impression that the orgy of railway building which the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has described was undertaken under the Borden regime. Borden came into power in 1911. The orgy of railway building in this country was, I think it can be said, in the first decade of the century. It is perfectly true that if we are talking about the setting up of the national railways, that did not come until after the first war. I do not dispute that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate was accurate in his statement. My only concern is with the name of a man for whom I have great respect, and I should not like the implication to remain that he alone was responsible for an error of judgment in proceeding too enthusiastically in the building of railways in the first decade of the century.

I lived in Manitoba from 1911 to 1914. I know there are many parts of Manitoba which would not have been opened up but for the work done by Sir William Mackenzie, Sir Donald Mann and Mr. D. B. Hanna, who really built the railroad. I must take slight exception to one of the statements made by the hon. member for Greenwood when he said that the orgy of railway building-and I myself would not have used that word-took place in the first decade of this century. The building continued until 1914 or 1915 and I think perhaps if the Borden government could have prevented the Canadian Northern Railway from going on to build a third line through northern Ontario some of those difficulties could have been overcome. However, that part of their line was built after the Borden government came into office and not before.
I do not believe anybody foresaw those things, but having that precedent we can foresee what might happen in the air line field and we shall be culpable in the eyes of posterity if we allow the same situation to arise with respect to air lines. That is my whole point.
Having made that point I wish to return to what I was saying with regard to an interjection made by the Minister of Transport- and perhaps if the debate going on alongside the Minister of Transport could cease the hon. gentleman would be able to hear what I am saying-

speechtext: Well, I shall not pursue that point. I was drawing attention, and because this is of such vast importance to

Supply-Transport
my constituency and to people in every fishing riding on the Atlantic coast I drew attention three times, and I am going to repeat the words used by the minister about small boats-
Before the hon. member goes on I wonder if he would answer a question about transportation.
Does the hon. member not regard boats as transportation?
Yes, but I was wondering whether the hon. member believes we should have a monopoly of air service in Canada now and in the future.
I can answer that question very easily. We have never had a monopoly. An intelligent decision was made by the Mackenzie King government at the end of the war, in the year 1944, which was carried on-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: I thought the war was still on in 1944.

The hon. member's colleague from Bow River asked a question to which I am sure he desires an answer. Perhaps if he could help me restrain some of his hon. friends I could give that answer. In 1944, when transcontinental air lines were in their infancy, when indeed there were no transcontinental air lines except T.C.A.-incidentally, the reason there were no others was that no one else felt it was worth while to have them-a decision was made that there should be only one instrument for international and transcontinental services for a considerable time to come, until we could see how this whole situation was going to develop. That was done precisely because Mr. C. D. Howe had had a long experience in connection with the railways and the problems which had been created by having services which were greater than the country could support. He had the wisdom not to want to have that kind of situation develop in the air.
I say without hesitation that if in order to have an air line which will be paid for by the users and not by the taxpayers we can only afford to have one in Canada, I am in favour of having only one.
A monopoly.

Yes, a monopoly; precisely. If you have two lines that are going to be bankrupt and subsidized by the treasury, or one line that can make money, I am in favour of one line that can make money, That is simple. If, on the other hand, you could have two lines that could both make

money, I think that is preferable. I think any sensible person with the kind of economic views I hold would take that view.
The worst of it is, nobody with the kind of economic views held by the hon. member could possibly be sensible.

That was a typical contribution from the learned member for Halifax. The point I am making is that what I am anxious to avoid is a subsidy on air travel, to any unnecessary extent, paid by the taxpayers of Canada. We know that with a sprawling country such as our own, with vast areas to open up and keep in contact with, some kind of subsidy will be necessary in some areas. In the national interest there have always been subsidies, and we shall have them for a long time to come. We should not try to maximize subsidization, we should try to minimize it; that is my position. It is a very simple, thrifty position. It is perhaps a little old fashioned, but I really believe that we should try to save the taxpayers' money. If that is a terrible confession to make in this house, I make it none the less, and am not ashamed to do so.
You have no monopoly on that.

Now, sir, there was not a monopoly on air services in Canada. The government decided that in other areas there would be opportunities given for free enterprise, and that these areas would be delineated through the medium of the air transport board, for which my friend the hon. member for Laurier was responsible during all its formative period. It did a splendid job in encouraging young men, who came out of the air force, to get into the air line business

relatively small companies-and gave them reasonable assurance that in the areas in which they became involved they would have the traffic, so there would be a reasonable chance for them to make these operations pay.
This policy represented a great contribution to that splendid decade of development we had in this country from 1946 to 1956, and it was most unfortunate, in my opinion, that the policy was abandoned by the former minister of transport. I hope the present minister will go back to it.
In so far as some of these services were concerned, I agree completely with what one hon. member on the other side of this house said earlier; this cutthroat competition which was allowed in this area has already driven quite a number of these air lines to the wall.

I did not intend to speak about this subject of air lines at all, because it is really not my field but that of my friend the hon. member for Laurier. All I know about it are the A B C's, which I learned from him. I was drawn into this subject as a result of one or two questions which were asked and I should like now to come back to the question of ships in connection with which, notwithstanding the fact that I lost mine, I still have a more immediate interest and concern.
Did you not receive any compensation for the loss of this ship?
It was insured by me under private enterprise, and I was fortunate enough to collect the insurance.
Was it a small boat or a big boat?

It was 110 feet long, and I leave it to the minister to decide whether it was small or big. The minister is not, even by indirection, going to get me to give any definition of what a small boat is, because that is exactly what I am trying to get him to do. The minister has said that the government intends to help the fishermen who are working in very small boats, and that it is going to look after them as well. The minister interjected yesterday during my remarks when I quoted him for the third time, and said, as found at page 5075 of Hansard for that date:
A boat 65 feet long is certainly not a big ship.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that is not the point involved. I do not know why he mentioned a boat 65 feet in length, because his policy includes boats from 45 feet in length. I suggest that a boat of even 45 feet, while it may not be a big ship, is not a small boat in the sense in which fishermen understand it; it is a large vessel. Small boats are a good deal smaller than that. The boats being used by the majority of fishermen are a good deal smaller than that.
The government's policy in this respect is to provide assistance for the operators of what we consider large fishing boats. While the government has done a great deal-this is a very serious criticism I have of the government, and I say at once that this criticism might be applied also to its predecessors-it has not done enough. Of course the public expected this government to correct all the errors of the previous government, not merely to excuse themselves because we had made them.
But you made so many.

I suggest the minister has a great opportunity now to do something
Supply-Transport
which we did not do. I suggest the difference between a man who fishes using a small boat and a man who fishes using these larger vessels is the difference between a family farm and a commercial farming operation. This government is doing something for the commercial fishing operation, but when the minister made his statement in this regard the other day he did not indicate any policy of providing assistance to what we might call the family fisherman, to adapt a phrase.
I should like to know whether this policy means that the government in fact is planning to assist owners of boats shorter than 45 feet and, if it is not, perhaps the minister could clear that up at once.
May I ask the hon. member a question?
If you will answer mine, you may.

Is he against the policy to provide an encouragement to the hon. member's fellow citizens of Newfoundland to own boats larger than 45 feet? I realize that many fishermen in Canada operating off our coasts use very small boats, but also that they face tremendous difficulties because they do so. We want to encourage people to build larger boats, and feel that bringing this legislation forward will encourage those individuals using the very small boats to use what we call a small boat but a little larger, that is to say boats between 45 and 65 feet in length.

What the minister is asking me is whether I object to having soup and dessert because I have asked for meat. Of course I am in favour of soup and dessert, but I am asking whether the minister is also going to provide the meat.
You are asking for gravy.

An hon. member has said something about gravy. I am referring to the government's policy and that may be his characterization of it, but it is not mine. I am very much in favour of the policy of assistance for fishing boats the minister has announced, which my hon. friend from Gloucester asked for the evening before it was announced. The policy announced by the minister provides something not quite as good as that asked for by the hon. member for Gloucester, but it is very nearly the same.
It is one o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, may I just finish my sentence? I am very much in favour of this assistance, but I am even more in favour of something being done to help the

Supply-Transport
inshore fishermen who, even with government assistance, could never raise the additional capital necessary to build these larger vessels; and I refer to the family fishermen.

The
hon. member's time expired at 12.50, but inasmuch as he was interrupted he may have the floor at 2.30, if that is the wish of the committee.

I feel that would be unfair, and that the floor should be given to someone else.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few brief comments at this time on the estimates of the Minister of Transport but before doing so I should like to join with the members who have preceded me in offering my congratulations to the minister on the leadership he has given to this department since assuming this office. He has indicated beyond any shadow of doubt that he is a minister who will look after the transportation problems that face this country and do so in a manner that will fully justify the promise he has shown through the years as a member of this house.
I wish to tell the minister just how happy the people in my part of the country are over the announcement he made on May 12 regarding assistance to the shipbuilding industry. This is a tremendous step in the right direction and will be of great benefit to the shipbuilding industry, to fisheries and to the people of this country who are seeking employment in those fields.
I might tell the minister I feel that further consideration should be given to the question of the assistance available in the construction of long-liners. Assistance is now available to long-liners between 45 feet and 65 feet in length. It may be that we should extend this assistance to a little larger type of wooden craft since, as the fishing industry has advanced, there has been a demand for a longer type of boat.
I might also make some mention of the recent cross fire between the minister and the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate regarding small boats. I do not think we need to extend the length of those vessels to the length of the luxury liner that the hon. member recently lost. I know he might

be anxious to look to the government for assistance in constructing a 110 foot vessel but-
They are covered; I was asking for the small ones.

-we would not want to go quite that far. At the same time the hon. member did refer to small vessels. I think the minister's explanation was that this assistance will allow those fishermen who today are not able to acquire craft of 45 feet in length to have the benefit of the subsidy, and it might very well put them in a position where they can acquire them. This is a forward step in that direction and one on which the minister should be congratulated.
If one looks over the budgets of the various provincial governments today one finds almost without exception that each shows a surplus. Unfortunately, this is not so with respect to the federal government because of the tremendous assistance provided to the provinces and to every aspect of our economy. If the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is interested in assisting the fishermen who are mainly involved in inshore fishing in smaller type vessels, maybe he can speak to his good friend the premier of Newfoundland who receives probably 65 per cent of his total budget from the federal government. It might be possible for him to take some small part of this and make it available to that type of fisherman.
I should also like to associate my remarks with those of the hon. member for Pictou. This very energetic member gives his constituency the type of representation it deserves. I refer also to the hon. member for Queens. Both of these hon. gentlemen have brought to the minister's attention the need for a replacement of the Charles A. Dunning ferry on the service between Pictou county and Prince Edward Island. There is no doubt that the people in Prince Edward Island deserve the very best service that the Canadian government can provide. The vessel to which I have referred is now outmoded, and the demand for ferry service in that area is such that consideration should certainly be given to the provision of a new vessel to take care of this very necessary service.
May I now turn to a matter of very urgent concern to my constituents in the disaster stricken town of Springhill. This has to do with the spur line between Springhill Junction and the town of Springhill. I should like to thank the minister for the very sympathetic consideration he has given to my requests on this particular subject, and also for the very sympathetic way in which the C.N.R. has

looked at this matter to date. It is a most complicated matter since the line is owned at present by a private company. The board of transport commissioners has indicated in a decision that they will allow the company to abandon the line, and since that time I have met with Mr. Gordon and the minister. I have discussed the matter with the premier of Nova Scotia who has also been in touch with the president of the C.N.R. and the minister. I am very hopeful that it will be possible to find some way for the C.N.R. to assume the operation of this spur line.
The request made by the citizens of the area is that only three and a half miles of the line be assumed by the C.N.R. This would mean that the town would have a railway line available to it when it was necessary to bring in materials. I might point out in this regard that a battery factory has recently been established there which almost of necessity needs the line to transport sulphuric acid from the junction.
The new coal mine established in Spring-hill, which is presently undertaking new developments in the area that will mean additional employment if they prove successful, could also benefit materially from the continued operation of the spur line. When a decision is reached on this matter I certainly hope it will be a favourable one assuring that Springhill will have the transportation facilities available to it that are necessary to attract new industry to the area.
I wish to turn to another problem of direct concern to my constituents, the re-establishment of a ferry service between Parrsboro and the Annapolis valley. There had been a ferry service in operation for 90 years until 1940 when the ferry which plied between Parrsboro and Kingsport was removed on the assumption that it could be utilized better in the war effort in another area of Canada. My constituents did not object at that time for it was their belief that they should do everything within their power to assist the war effort. However, at the end of the war they quickly realized that what had been taken from them was not to be returned. This was most unfortunate and it became even more so as the years went by for the beautiful town of Parrsboro found itself cut off from the main transportation route upon the establishment of the trans-Canada highway in another area of my constituency. Since that time the people there have made many efforts to have the ferry service re-established.
I might say it is to the credit of the government that very serious consideration was given to the establishment of a scheduled
Supply-Transport
service between Cumberland and the Annapolis valley. However, this meant the construction of deep-water piers. Estimates of the cost of construction varied between $6 million and $10 million, and in the light of the circumstances involved the Minister of Public Works found that he was unable to provide this amount. As a result, only recently those interested in this service have been making efforts to have consideration given to the re-establishment of a tidal ferry service. If this were done a study could be made of the traffic available and it could then be determined whether it would be feasible to make an expenditure of the size needed to build deep-water piers.
I should like to bring to the minister's attention the fact that the Nova Scotia government has two ferries at the present time which will be available for other uses this fall when the bridge over the Bras d'Or lakes is completed. These two ferries are the John Cabot, which could handle between 20 and 22 motor cars, and the Percy C. Black named after a former member for Cumberland. He was an outstanding member of the House of Commons and the Nova Scotia legislature for many years and made a tremendous contribution to the history of Canada. If these two vessels could be altered they could be utilized in this service.
I am informed by the provincial government that the necessary alterations would cost about $100,000. This is a fairly large expenditure, one that it would be difficult for the provincial government to undertake by itself although that government did indicate that if the federal government would construct the piers they would be willing to undertake the alterations of these two vessels. Since the federal government is in my belief obligated to replace this ferry service and has indicated that it will not agree to an expenditure of the size necessary for the construction of deep-water piers, it is my view that it should be willing to enter into an agreement with the provincial government in order to assist it in the alterations necessary to make these two ferries satisfactory for this service.
I might point out to the minister that in the 90 years during which the ferry service was available to my constituents and the people of the Annapolis valley the federal government made available a subsidy of between $4,000 and $5,000 per year to assist in the operation of the service. Since the federal government has been fortunate enough to save this sum for some 20-odd years, it seems

Supply*-Transport
only right that ways and means might be considered of making at least a portion of this amount available to the provincial government to carry out the alterations necessary to prepare these ferries for this service. I understand that the facilities at Kingsport would have to be extended.
I might point out that the Minister of Public Works has recently seen the completion of a very fine new wharf at Parrsboro, and repairs are presently under way on the breakwater in that area. This means that with a slight expenditure we would probably be able to have facilities available in the Parrsboro area which would be satisfactory for the loading and unloading of motor vehicles. I would appreciate the minister giving very serious consideration to this proposed ferry service because it will mean a great deal to the economy of Parrsboro, Parrsboro Shore and the area of Five Islands in the constituency of my good friend the hon. member for Colchester-Hants.
I might point out also that the federal government has recently made available to the province of Nova Scotia a contribution of 50 per cent of the cost of the construction of a new highway along the Parrsboro Shore. It would only seem logical to me, since we have now spent approximately $300,000 of our own money to prepare these tourist roads, that we should make every possible effort to attract the tourists to this area. Certainly, the re-establishment of this ferry service would be the best possible way of doing that. In my opinion, this would be of tremendous assistance to the agriculture industry in both the Annapolis valley and Cumberland. It eliminates at least 115 miles from the route between Annapolis valley and the New Brunswick border. There is no doubt but that any possible means of getting our goods closer to the market is something that deserves serious consideration.
I believe those are the two main items I wish to bring to the minister's attention. I should like to again offer him my thanks for the assistance he has made available to both the shipping and fishing industries of my province.
(Translation):

Would you allow me, Mr. Chairman, to tender, as did the previous speaker, my congratulations and wishes to the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) on his appointment to the post of minister of the important department he now administers.
I wish him as much success as had his predecessors having particularly in mind the

hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier), promoter of the St. Lawrence seaway, which is the envy of every other country since its necessity, its economic soundness and opportunities are being realized.
The hon. member for Laurier has so put his stamp on that department that whenever the estimates of the Department of Transport are discussed, we can rightly wonder whether hon. members on the government benches do not still consider him as the minister in charge.
The policy announced to the house in connection with ship operating and shipbuilding on Friday, May 12 last, and I quote the very words of the minister:
-is intended to make it possible for Canadian ship operators to obtain new vessels from Canadian shipyards at reasonable and competitive prices instead of being forced to have them built abroad because of the lower construction costs that prevail in other countries.
This is a commendable policy and is to the credit of the government. However, the way it was introduced and the method of its implementation leave some doubt as to its legality.
On the same date, the minister advised the house that:
Parliament will be asked to provide, by way of departmental estimates, funds-
For the purposes set forth in his statement. I wonder whether this procedure is in accordance with the spirit of the constitution.
In the same statement, the minister advised the house that:
The methods of determining approved costs for this purpose and other particulars relating to administration of this plan will be prescribed by regulations to be approved by the governor in council.
But how could the governor in council make regulations unless they can apply to an act duly approved by parliament?
As an example, I refer you to chapter 294 of the Revised Statutes of Canada under which the government first received authorization from parliament before granting subsides to wheat producers. Because of that authorization, which took the form of an act, the governor in council could then make the appropriate regulations.
To those remarks, which are made in a spirit of co-operation, I add the wish that the proposed policy of the minister will bring back to our shipyards the prosperity of former years and provide to hundreds of voters in my constituency an opportunity to resume the jobs they lost when the yards closed down.

Mr. Chairman, with your permission, I would now like to add a few brief remarks relating to certain matters which were brought to the attention of the Minister of Transport May 18 last, by my colleague from Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschate-lets). Like the Maisonneuve-Rosemont riding, the Hochelaga constituency, that I represent in this house, borders, in all its width, to the southeast, on the St. Lawrence river. It is crossed throughout from west to east by the C.N.R. railway tracks, and its western boundary is located a few blocks from Jacques Cartier bridge.
You will realize, from those preliminary remarks, that the welfare of the people in the Hochelaga riding can be affected to a great extent by the policy implemented by the Department of Transport.
I shall deal first of all with the railway lines operated by the C.N.R. Those lines extend from Moreau street, former location of the station of that same name, and cross Hochelaga riding from the southwest to the northeast.
They were built in 1913 by the Canadian Northern Quebec Railways Company. At that time, this section of Montreal island was part of the town of Maisonneuve which was annexed to the city of Montreal toward the end of the second decade of this century. At that time, those tracks ran through vacant lots, crossed by a few streets with only a few houses on them.
At the time, the population of the area affected by those railway tracks did not exceed a few thousand, but is now over 200,000.
Since this trackage was taken over by the C.N.R., the topography of that section of Montreal has completely changed by reason of the growth in population and consequent development.
Many new streets were opened up. Countless residential, business and public buildings, as well as churches and schools, have been built.
Those lines were built for two specific purposes: a daily transport service, both ways, by three passenger trains, one of which ran up to Chicoutimi, and freight transport, a small amount of which was intended for the few factories established along the lines. The other freight cars were directed to other lines, farther west, to be exchanged or handed over to the Canadian Pacific Railways.
It is undeniable that the presence of those railway tracks explains the lag in the development of this part of Montreal, as compared to other parts of the island.

Railway trackage within cities has never been considered as an attraction. Freight trains are unsightly, they are noisy; they hold up both pedestrian and automobile traffic. All this, together with the direct hazard they are for citizens who use the streets intersected by those railway lines have been, since 1913, so many unattractive features which, as we are now regretfully compelled to realize, have hindered the progress of this eastern part of the city of Montreal.
It happens that the purpose for which those railway tracks were built no longer exists today.
Moreau station disappeared 15 years ago. Passenger trains using that station as a terminal at the time have been rerouted and now operate out of Central station.
Except in a very few cases, freight trains use the elevated tracks situated more to the north on the island of Montreal.
It means that these tracks between Moreau and Viau streets are only there now to serve some 20 manufacturers which could as easily use another means for shipping and receiving goods.
They are also used by tank-cars from oil refineries in Montreal east. These could and should use another existing route by merely making a few changes.
When you consider the lay-out of those tracks, you can see that between Moreau and Viau streets they cross more than 25 streets, which means as many level crossings.
Now, the area comprised between those 25 streets is one of the most thickly populated on Montreal island.
Whether they go to church, to school or want to take the nearest bus, those people have to cross the railroad tracks.
One can imagine the dangers and the delays resulting from those level crossings which for a few years now have even been gateless.
About traffic hold-ups I have a very definite case for the minister's attention.
I live on Prefontaine street, a few hundred feet north of those railroad tracks. I can assure him that the traffic is held up daily on account of the freight cars running on those tracks, some times for half an hour -and this in spite of many representations made to the Canadian National authorities and to the predecessor of the present minister and in open and repeated violation of section 314 of the Railway Act which limits such periods of obstruction to five minutes.

My colleague, the member for Maison-neuve-Rosemont, and myself supported by the association of Montreal east businessmen, are again asking the Minister of Transport to ask the Canadian National to reconsider their decision and to give up using those railroad tracks which have become practically unnecessary and unprofitable compared to the loss and lessening of welfare inflicted upon a population of over 200,000 persons. This population must suffer all the inconvenience resulting from the existence and operation of those tracks, because some reluctance is being experienced when it comes to withdrawing the privilege of a siding granted to a score of industries that use it only occasionally.

Mr. Chairman, I should like now to take up another matter which has to do with the item before us, the need for a new bridge east of Jacques Cartier bridge.
At the present time, Montreal and the south shore of the St. Lawrence are linked by three bridges: Jacques Cartier bridge, Victoria bridge which is the property of the C.N.R., and Mercier bridge which is under provincial jurisdiction.
A fourth one, Champlain bridge, is under construction.
To sum it up, even if Montreal east has a much larger population than Montreal west-although the count is difficult-it has only one bridge, the Jacques Cartier bridge to which have been added the two lanes reserved to street cars at the time the bridge was built. Those two lanes have alleviated the problem created by the unbelievably rapid and continuing growth of recent years in the number of motor vehicles using that bridge.
But they are by no means the solution the public which is also the taxpayer are entitled to expect from the government about such an urgent and important problem.
Indeed, on both shores of the St. Lawrence river, below the Jacques Cartier bridge, we have seen an industrial, commercial and residential development which upsets all forecasts of only 30 years ago planned to promote connecting roads between them.
The new plants built or under construction on the north shore, and especially on the
