speechtext: I think it is the latter.
You mean an action against the insurance company?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: My recollection is that the damages for $8,300, were paid by the insurance company. I do not see reference to this in the editorial, but I am of the impression that the insurance company, under a subrogation clause contained in the contract, instituted proceedings against the air lines.
It would not be of much use to take out an insurance policy for $100,000, would it?
That is a different thing involving a contract between two persons.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I think there is another point involved which arises, because it depends on where the individual is going. This is a case affecting an international flight, wherein the Warsaw convention, and not protocol, was brought in as a defence in United States courts, and was successful in that not more than $8,300 should be paid the plaintiff.
(Translation):

At the outset of my remarks, Mr. Chairman, I should like, on behalf of my constituents, to commend the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) and to tell him how proud we are of his appointment to the post of Minister of Transport. He deserves our heartiest congratulations for the efficient manner in which he heads his department.
(Text):
The policies of certain branches of the Department of Transport deeply affect my constituents who are, and I think justly so, very interested in any action taken by the government in so far as it affects their transportation problems, especially those of the sea.
This island gem sits in the centre of the gulf of St. Lawrence, and has faced transportation problems for many years.

Supply-Transport
Some 50 years ago the first mode of transportation from the island to the mainland was the launching of a cask in which was placed a letter addressed to the postmaster general of Canada informing him of the immediate need for steamship connections between the mainland and the islands. This letter also requested that if they could not send the answer by boat to send it back in the same cask. If I am forced to speak about those problems today it is because of an article appearing in La Presse of Montreal some three days ago, which is entitled:
(Translation):
Quebec approaches Ottawa-Answer being sought to the problem of the Magdalen Islands.
(Text):
The minister of transport and communications of the province of Quebec was telling the Quebec legislature that he was coming to Ottawa to solve the water transportation problems of the people of my constituency. I had never intended to tell this house about the problem and what this government has done toward a partial solution of this water transportation difficulty. During the fiscal year 1960-61 the federal government contributed to Clarke Steamship, which operated a passenger-freight service between Montreal, Quebec, Gaspe and the Magdalen islands, a subsidy in the amount of $259,077. The provincial government contributed $64,700 as a subsidy to this transportation company. In the same year the federal government paid to the Magdalen Islands Transportation Company, operating from Pictou to the island as well as Charlottetown to the island, a subsidy in the amount of $174,000 and in the same year to C.T.M.A., operating from the Magdalen islands an amount of $6,667 for service between Chetieamp and Halifax. Clarke Steamship withdrew their services from Montreal to Quebec to the islands because of the decision of the Canadian maritime commission that no more subsidy should be paid owing to the fact that there were alternative, better or cheaper, means of transportation. The Magdalen Island Transportation Company also withdrew their boat plying between Pictou and the island because of its age, and the C.T.M.A. existing service in that area has plied between Chetieamp and Halifax for many years. The people of those islands have been requesting better transportation to and from the islands from various governments. As the committee will readily realize, there are only two possibilities, transportation either by air or by sea. The people requested more frequent trips between the islands and different ports in the maritime provinces, and also a better boat to carry cars to and from the island.
[Mr. Keays.l
Over a number of years many petitions were sent to different governments and this year this government acceded to the request by inviting different transportation companies to tender on the service between Pictou and the islands, Charlottetown and the islands, Souris and the islands. Clarke Steamships were the lowest tenderers and received permission to do this work and also a subsidy of $298,000.
This has been a great improvement in so far as transportation to the island is concerned, Mr. Chairman, because it permits the transportation of passengers and freight as well as making it possible to bring fresh meat to the island owing to the existence of refrigeration on the ship North Gaspe. Instead of having two trips per week they now have three, and during the months of July, August and possibly September, four trips from the mainland to the islands. Let me assure you, Mr. Chairman, this is appreciated by the people of the islands and it gives them an opportunity to get out during the fine season of the year or to have their relatives visit them during the same season.
However, there are other problems which arise when you wish to have more frequent trips. One of these problems has been the elimination of the stop at Grande Entree on the east end of the island. I do hope that eventually this problem will be solved and that the government's wish to improve greatly the service will be realized and that, if requested, a study will be made of the possibility of operating a roll-on roll-off boat service to the Magdalen islands. When this happens I hope that many of the water transportation problems will be solved.
Apart from the subsidy of $298,000 granted to the Clarke Steamship Company, there is also another service which has been subsidized, namely the one operating between the Magdalen islands and Halifax passing through Chetieamp, Nova Scotia. The C.T.M.A. have received a subsidy of $30,000 to operate this service. They have also received a subsidy of $30,000 to operate a service between Isle Madame, Guysborough and Canso, Nova Scotia. At the moment this is strictly a freight service, but I am sure that with the new policy enunciated by the Minister of Transport recently concerning subsidies toward the construction of ships that the people who operate this service will take advantage of these grants to build other ships to give bigger and better service to those islands so far off the shores of the mainland.
There has also been another subsidy granted, and that was for a service in the gulf. The federal contribution to this service is roughly $42,500. Another subsidy is also being promised to another service between

Montreal, Gaspe and the gulf. Naturally this subsidy is conditional upon the province paying an equal or larger amount.
The geographical position of the Magdalen islands forces the people there to bring in much of their merchandise from maritime ports. However, in turn the maritime provinces take fish products from our islands. You will realize, therefore, that the federal government has made a very large contribution toward the solution of the water transportation problems in my constituency.
The only other problem that seems to be of any concern is the transportation of passengers from the cities of Montreal and Quebec to the islands. I believe this can be accomplished much better by improving the air service to the islands. Unfortunately the provincial government thought it right to cancel the subsidy previously granted to a local air transportation firm operating out of Gaspe, namely, Trans-Gaspesian Air Lines, and as a result of this action the air line will eventually be forced out of business. The people of the Magdalen islands are eager to maintain their relations with the people of the province of Quebec generally and are able to travel by this air line between the mainland of Quebec and the islands. If the government of the province of Quebec is deeply concerned about the passenger transportation problem and if the minister of transport and communications of the province of Quebec is going to come to Ottawa for additional subsidies to carry merchandise to the islands, I suggest to the Minister of Transport that possibly he should go to Quebec and ask his counterpart in the provincial legislature to contribute something toward the transportation of people to the islands.
While the article in question is not in a sense derogatory so far as the federal government is concerned, I note that there is an impression that the federal government has not done anything with regard to the transportation problems I have mentioned. Let me point out, Mr. Chairman, that during the year 1960-61 the federal government contributed by way of subsidies directly affecting the islands an amount of $439,744 while the provincial contribution was $104,700. During the year 1961-62 to date the federal government has contributed $420,500 but now no grant is given by the provincial government. I believe the provincial government should also contribute to the bettering of the transportation services between the islands and the mainland.
It may also be interesting to note that to date the federal government has contributed to the province of Quebec a total of $821,123 in subsidies. I will admit that the province 90205-6-324J
Supply-Transport
is always looking for more but I believe the federal government has made a very worthwhile contribution.
May I ask the hon. member a question? Is the total figure he gave of $821,123 on a yearly basis?

It is on a yearly basis. Before resuming my seat I should like to commend the officers of the Canadian maritime comission who have the tremendous task of deciding exactly what amount of subsidy shall be recommended for any petitioner. All hon. members will know that the subsidies are based on the difference between revenue and the operation, depreciation and administration costs of the ship in question. I think that this year the federal government has done a remarkable job in that the Minister of Transport has saved the federal treasury an amount of approximately $60,000 while at the same time providing these people with better transportation facilities. Examples such as this are common with this government and I hope they will continue to be.

Mr. Chairman, since the time this afternoon is obviously going to be used up anyway, there seems to be a good deal of reason for having some of it used by the opposition. I have some things I wish to say and I will dispense with congratulations to the minister. I might make a suggestion to the minister through you, Mr. Chairman. Possibly he might ask all his colleagues to have their congratulations simply printed in Hansard without being delivered in the house because I am sure we could save at least a day in the session this year.
You should do likewise with your congratulations of yourself.

The hon. member says that any congratulations I make of myself might be omitted. They will be. I noticed the interest that the hon. member for St. John's East showed in the subsidies that the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine pointed out were being paid annually to the various services in the province of Quebec. I am sure what was going through the hon. member's mind was what went through my mind at that moment, namely, what an extraordinary long time it has taken the treasury board to complete consideration of the proposal for an east coast ferry that was before treasury board in August of 1959 during the course of the provincial election in Newfoundland.
At that time, as the hon. member for St. John's East and the hon. member for St. John's West will no doubt both recall, the then leader of the Conservative party in Newfoundland made a public statement to

Supply-Transport
which I wish to refer. I am not sure whether he is still leader of the Conservative party. He is not in the legislature and I do not think they have bothered to choose a leader since. In any event, when Mr. Hollett was the leader he made the public statement-
Would the hon. member permit me to interject to keep the record straight?
I am not so sure I would not rather have the interjection without the extra phrase because I do not think it will keep the record straight.

First of all, Mr. Chairman, I referred at length to the east coast ferry in my remarks yesterday, I believe, during this debate. My main reason for interjecting at this point is to deal with the hon. member's reference to the previous leader of the Conservative party in Newfoundland. He was in fact the house leader and we have a house leader of the party right now in Newfoundland.
In other words, I was quite correct that there is no leader of the Conservative party in Newfoundland at all. That is what I suspected.
On the contrary.

It is too confusing for me, sir, and no doubt that is why it is so confusing for the electors of Newfoundland. Whether they have a leader or whether they have not a leader seems to make very little difference. This, I realize, has nothing to do with the minister's estimates. What has to do with the minister's estimates is that this very estimable gentleman, Mr. Hollett, who was in the last legislature but is not in this one, gave a solemn assurance to the people of Newfoundland that, at the very moment, the treasury board was giving consideration- that was two years ago-to a proposal for an east coast ferry. So far as we know, the east coast ferry is a lot farther from the treasury board now than it was then. I am just wondering if there is any real project for an east coast ferry or if the government intends to wait until after the final decision has been made about the dissolution of this parliament to give us another promise for another election.
The hon. member should ask his colleague how long it took to get the Carson on the go.

I know how long it took to get the Carson on the go. I know some of the reasons why it took so long to get the Carson on the go. As the hon. gentleman knows full well, there is nothing on the drawing boards or anywhere else in respect

of this east coast ferry. There is still argument as to whether or not one will be built at all. I have no doubt that every time the question gets anywhere near the Minister of Finance he turns thumbs down on it. I have no doubt, sir, that as has happened with so many other projects, the only time we will hear anything that appears to be definite about this project will be about the time of dissolution of this parliament. Even then, it will be pretty "iffy", as most of these promises are.
However, the point about which I rose to speak was something quite different. I merely referred to this because, like the hon. member for St. John's East, I was rather struck by the disparity between the wonderful treatment given to the Magdalen islands, according to the member.
We have not got a good air service.

I know the hon. gentleman wants still more. At the present time, the government seems more concerned about improving the service between the Magdalen islands and Prince Edward Island than it is about giving that air service to the Magdalen islands the hon. member asks for. Perhaps if the hon. member would resign his seat and cause a by-election, he could get that air service for the Magdalen islands. Perhaps he would not think that too great a sacrifice to make. He could emulate his colleague the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska, who is reputedly getting an airport for his constituency, although nobody knows where that airport will be built. I suspect nothing more will be heard about it after May 29.
To whom is the hon. member referring?
I was referring to that gentleman to whom the Prime Minister always referred as "my friend Charlie, who is so badly needed in this house".
The hon. member has been talking so much about resigning that I thought perhaps he was thinking of resigning.

What I rose to speak about, sir, was the service given in Newfoundland by Canadian National Telegraphs. Under the terms of union, the telegraph and telephone services, which were operated by the department of posts, telephones and telegraphs of Newfoundland, were taken over as a federal service by the federal government. The telephone services, apart from those telephone services that were provided by the Avalon Telephone Company and one or two other companies, were taken over by Canadian National Telegraphs. I know there has been some criticism of Canadian National

Telegraphs and I have, at times, criticized them myself, even when I was in office. However, I do want to say here that I think this organization has made a tremendous effort-on the whole a successful effort-to improve service in Newfoundland.
Since we came into office.

Ever since 1949. I have noticed no difference whatever, for the better or worse, since the hon. gentlemen came into office. I assume that hon. gentlemen opposite treat the Canadian National Telegraphs in the same way as their predecessors did, that is there is no political interference. I assume that, and I hope my assumption is correct.
You should know it is correct.

I do not know it is correct because obviously the hon. member for St. John's West, the Solicitor General, was trying to imply it was not correct and there was some political interference. He was implying this government had done something about it that had not been done by the previous government.
I am interjecting to say that I think the hon. member has no cause to complain against Canadian National Telegraphs. They are doing a good job in his district.

They are doing a good job all over Newfoundland, and that is exactly what I was saying. There seems to be no quarrel between the hon. gentleman and me, except possibly in semantics and, perhaps, that is an obstacle to communications. As the hon. gentleman knows, there are much more serious obstacles to communications in Newfoundland than semantics. There are tremendous practical difficulties in the building up of communications in Newfoundland.
When I say that I am not complaining about Canadian National Telegraphs but on the contrary I am commending them for the tremendous improvements that have been made since 1949, both in telegraph and telephone service I am rising to make a suggestion to the minister. I know that we on this side are accused by the government of making no practical suggestions. I have a highly practical suggestion to make to the government, and it is this. As a part of next winter's winter works program, the government should undertake a real blitz in Newfoundland to expand telegraph and telephone service, especially telephone service. The only reason they are not expanded faster is that Canadian National Telegraphs have a certain budget each year; that is the only reason.
Now, eight or nine years after confederation, when everybody knows that because of
Supply-Transport
Korea and other things, there was a tremendous shortage of electronic and telephone equipment and it was very hard to get. This is not the case today. There is no lack of any of the things that are necessary to modernize the telephone and telegraph services except money. There is labour there. There is timber in Newfoundland, and there are the plants on the mainland which make the wire and the instruments. Everything that is needed is available in this country, and the lack is enough money. I believe the Canadian National Telegraphs, like the Canadian National Railways system, is supposed to be run as a business enterprise. I approve of that. They should be run as business enterprises, and if possible they should pay. However, the Canadian National Telegraphs cannot be expected to bear the burden of any additional costs which would be incurred by putting on a real push.
What I am going to suggest to the government is this. The government, as a winter works program, could pay half the labour cost of all the additional work that the Canadian National Telegraphs could do in order to modernize in all parts of Newfoundland, just as if the Canadian National Telegraphs were a municipality. In that way they could keep down their costs. The government could also provide an additional budget for next year as part of this program to stimulate employment, and they could get on with this job a great deal faster than has been possible with the limited budget up until now.
If this were done, two things could very well be undertaken in the wintertime as well or better than at any other time. One would be to get out the poles. It would be far better to do that in the wintertime, but you cannot get out the poles unless you know for sure they are going to be used next year to open up the lines. Also the stretching of the lines could be done just as well in the winter as any other time.
Mr. Chairman, does the hon. member seriously mean that?
Yes, I do seriously mean that, and this is a subject about which I am reasonably well informed.
The hon. member is endorsing our winter works program.
No, but I am suggesting a winter works program that would really work.
It would be on the same principle as our program.
I am suggesting-

I think the hon. member is right; it was a great success.

Supply-Transport

Mr. Chairman, I really cannot object very much to the minister interrupting me occasionally because I myself have been known to interrupt once or twice in the house. But of course I did not say anything of the kind.
You never do.

I have said, and I say again, that the winter works program is inadequate, but I have never condemned the winter works program in itself; I have merely said it is inadequate. I am trying to suggest to the minister one way in which he should give his colleagues, the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Finance-he is the real obstacle, as we all know-a real push and make the winter works program much more adequate than it now is.
The difficulty we have in Newfoundland- and it is greater than in any other province, as hon. members from Newfoundland know- is that there are very few organized municipalities. In Newfoundland there are not the means of providing work in the areas where it is most needed. I refer to the outports of Newfoundland. There are not, in most cases, the means of having these shared programs with the municipalities.
However, there is in the C.N.T. an organization which urgently needs to be modernized; they urgently need this modernization speeded up. They are well capable of directing this activity; they have very competent officers. This would give them no difficulty. I wager that if they were told now, not next fall, that their budget was going to be doubled-it is no use telling them next October

they would get ready and obtain the men and contractors to do this job.
They could have the men organized to get the poles out and get the whole thing planned so that this job could be done on a much larger scale than has been the case in the past. It would cut down the drain on the unemployment insurance fund and relief; it would give useful work to a great many men during the fall, winter and spring, and it would provide a service which pays when it is provided in most parts of Newfoundland. It is not as though this service were losing money. Most of the C.N.T. service in Newfoundland is a paying proposition. I will admit that there are a few lines into a few remote places which do not pay, but most of them do.
Therefore this would not be wasting money, as we have to waste it now on relief and get no return for it.
The Solicitor General does not agree.

I do not care very much whether or not the Solicitor General agrees. I am dealing with facts, facts that are very

well known to those of us with experience of the outports of Newfoundland.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: Do you not have snow and frost there in the wintertime?

Of course there is snow and frost there, but as the hon. gentlemen must know-it has been true in the history of Canada for 300 years-men have gone out into the woods in the wintertime to cut timber. There is nothing new about that; and that is one of the biggest parts of this proposal for speed up and expansion of the C.N.T. capital program.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate must have misunderstood me. I was referring to building lines in the wintertime. I suggest that the hon. member's province has some snow and frost and it may be difficult.
One always has snow and frost in the winter.

One does not always have snow and frost in the winter, notwithstanding what my colleague, the hon. member for Essex East, has said. Three winters ago, when we had a premature election foisted upon the people of this country, there was no frost and snow in Newfoundland until after the end of March. Hon. gentlemen know that well and thank heaven there was not, because it would have made it impossible for them to have carried out their campaign. There are often open winters of that kind in Newfoundland.
However, the fact that the ground is frozen is not at all an obstacle to the building of a line. It is very frequently much more difficult in the springtime, when the roads are soft and when the bogs are wet, to do these things than it is in the wintertime.
The fact of the matter is, as I have just been reminded by my colleague from Laurier, that a radar line was built in Newfoundland in the wintertime not so very long ago. A great deal of construction goes on now all over this country in the wintertime.
I say that if the government, through this winter works program, would make a contribution to the labour costs, and if they would increase or, say, double the budget of the C.N.T. and really get on with this job, it would be a contribution to the economy of Newfoundland and would reduce the number of unemployed next winter. Also, it would be a largely self-liquidating project.
Mr. Chairman, would the hon. gentleman permit a question?
Certainly.
Why did not my hon. friend's party undertake this program when they were in office from 1949 to 1957?

I have already answered that question, but I will be delighted to answer it again for the benefit of the hon. gentleman, who apparently was not following very carefully.
In that period there were two very good reasons why this was not done. Up until about two years before the former government went out of office there was a shortage of electronic equipment and other equipment of that sort. I know this very well because I was pressing the C.N.T. all through this time to modernize, and they could not do it because they could not get the equipment.
But this has not been true since about 1955 or 1956. However, as everybody knows, in the years 1955 and 1956 there was no serious problem of unemployment, even in the winters of 1955-6 and 1956-7.
Oh, oh.
Of course, that is why there was no-
Oh, oh.

Well, the statistics have been put on the record often enough that if the hon. gentlemen could learn, they would have learned that fact long ago. This is precisely why the people of this country are so fed up with Her Majesty's present advisers. We did not have winter works programs, because they were not needed. I hope I have answered the hon. gentleman's question.
Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member permit a question?
Certainly.
Would the hon. member say whether he has any old lumber on his own property in Newfoundland that he would offer for use as telephone poles?

I regret to have to say that although I own a house in Newfoundland, I do not own the land on which the house is situated; it is merely leased. So there would be no way, that I can see, in which I could possibly profit by this program except as a Canadian citizen.

Mr. Chairman, if the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate will allow me, I should just like to say one word of congratulation to the minister on the fine work he has done in introducing the shipbuilding program. This will be very beneficial to the west coast of Canada. I am sure the
Supply-Transport
minister is doing an exceptionally good job in the position he is now occupying. That is perhaps worrying the opposition a little bit, but I am sure the minister will be there a long time and as time goes on his stature will increase. I wish him all the luck in the world in his new position.
In British Columbia we have quite a sizeable river, the Fraser, which I think is as important to the province of British Columbia and the west coast of Canada as the St. Lawrence is to the east coast. Undoubtedly, in the last number of years, many years as a matter of fact, I do not think it has ever been recognized as being of the importance that it has, and has never had the same consideration as has been given to the ports of eastern Canada. However, I think this government, from what they have told me, have recognized its importance and are going to see it gets a square deal. It is undoubtedly the largest fresh water all year round port in North America and possibly one of the best fresh water and year round ports in the entire world.
In the last calendar year the port of Westminster-actually it is called New Westminster-which is the home port of the Fraser river, has had close to 600 deep-sea ships and with a little bit of development it could triple its importance; and now with the great work that the Minister of Agriculture is doing in selling wheat to the Orient, with a little further development the Fraser river could become the Liverpool of North America.
There are some 70 miles of deep-sea shipping facilities on both sides of the river. That would make approximately 140 miles of potential docks and in the municipalities of the delta, Richmond, Surrey, New Westminster, Coquitlam, Langley and possibly Maple Ridge, there are thousands of acres bordering the river which are ideally suited for industrial plants. I am sure the municipalities there are willing to co-operate with the government in the development of the river and the development of this land. True, we have the port of Vancouver but it has got fairly well filled up and the only place on the lower mainland to go for a real port is the Fraser river which requires development.
Since coming to this house I have been advocating to the department the establishment of a Fraser river harbour commission or a Fraser river authority with jurisdiction over the deep or navigable part of the river. I would urge the minister-I know he is well aware of this because I have spoken to his officials on several occasions-to establish this commission with representation as wide as possible from the municipalities which are interested in the establishment of the

Supply-Transport
ports on the Fraser river. In any of these areas if there is an industry established or any development done it helps that portion of the area as well as all the lower part of the mainland of British Columbia.
I should like to bring to the attention of the minister a matter which has already been referred to on several occasions, namely the menace which the present river bridge creates to river navigation where it crosses the Fraser at New Westminster. This bridge is a swing span which narrows down the channel for deep-sea ships. I realize it is an old bridge and possibly not worth while spending a great deal of money on but I would suggest that consideration be given to building a new bridge possibly in a different location because the one that is there now is in the wrong location. If not, and the old bridge is suitable for years to come, I would suggest the minister give consideration to taking out the swing span and putting in a lift span so as to improve the navigable part of that river.
I should also like to bring to the minister's attention the proposed Brookswood airport site which is in southern Surrey, two miles from the international boundary. I understand this is the most fog-free part of the whole Fraser valley, or of the west coast as far as that is concerned, and would make an ideal site for a light plane base or a supplementary airport to Vancouver airport. I think it would be good business on the part of the government to purchase this land before it is built on or developed because it is the only place of any size that is available in the whole area and it will be much cheaper to buy now than some day in the future when the area has been developed and this part of the country has been built up. Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

It is with a great deal of satisfaction I follow my hon. friend from New Westminster. We in British Columbia stick strongly together, and it is a pleasure to be following him at this time. With the permission of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate I should like to extend my sincere congratulations to the Minister of Transport and, if I may, to congratulate him on his patience in enduring the many suggestions he has received in the past several days. I think the diversity of the suggestions, their depth and number, indicates the size and importance of the Department of Transport.
I should like to draw his attention to one or two matters which I think are of prime importance. First, I want to say that I think one of the most significant and important speeches made recently was the one given by the Prime Minister at the convocation at Dalhousie on May 19 during the course of

which he made the suggestion that an international space agency be set up-an agency which would be representative of scientists, lawyers and educational institutions, one which would have the objective of safeguarding free and equal access by all nations for space exploration.
The Prime Minister made what I consider to be another sound suggestion, and that is the establishment of an international space year, in his words, so that a full study may be made of the demilitarization and utilization of outer space.
How does this come under these estimates, interesting as the subject matter is?

I thank the hon. member for Essex East for his remark and I shall now show him the connection. I wish to refer to the remarks of the hon. member for Laurier. At page 4759 of Hansard he indicated he thought the transport department should be divided into two parts and in his suggestion he thought there should be a minister of air and, of course, a minister of railways and canals. A similar suggestion was made by Mr. Grant McConachie, president of the Canadian Pacific Airlines several months ago. I think the hon. member for Laurier took the attitude he did primarily on the basis of a breakdown of the work load. As a former minister of transport he realizes the extensiveness of the department and the burden on the minister. But I should like to approach this from a different aspect. I agree that there should be a breakdown in the department but 1 should like to see the establishment of a minister of aeronautics and space. The minister of that department would have the responsibility for all matters dealing with civil aviation, telecommunications and meteorology, as well as the workings of the national research council in respect of space development. I understand too it is hoped that Canada will send a satellite into space using a United States rocket for propulsion and I think this type of work would come under the direction of a minister of such a department.
Perhaps hon. members are wondering why I suggest this at this particular time. I do so because I feel Canada is in a unique position. The city of Montreal is the centre for the international civil aviation organization and the international air transport association, both of which are vitally concerned with travel in space. The McGill institute of air and space law is also located in the city of Montreal. Coincidental with this, we have two or three large prestige buildings being constructed in Montreal at the present time, and I would suggest that

one of these, such as Place Ville Marie, would be the location for the organization such as the Prime Minister has suggested. I do not believe this organization could be situated in a better place than Montreal. Canada is a nation of rationality and neutrality and, considering that along with the fact that these two world-wide organizations, I.C.A.O. and I.A.T.A. are already established in Montreal, which indicates the importance of that city, with its proximity to New York and the United Nations, I feel that this is sufficient justification for this important step. I feel that the Canadian government should take the steps necessary to establish such a ministry.
I suggest Canada has already taken the leadership in establishing these organizations in Montreal, and should again take the leadership by organizing an international space year, and thereby assist in establishing Canada's leadership among the nations of the world. The international geophysical year produced excellent scientific co-operation among the scientists of the world, and I suggest that similar co-operation will follow the organization of an international space year. I suggest that this should be brought about as soon as possible, and that Canada should take the lead in this field.
I should now like to turn to matters of perhaps purely local concern. In British Columbia there exists what is known as the Vancouver international airport, although it is located on Sea island, just outside the city of Vancouver, entirely within the municipality of Richmond. On June 21 of this year we are having another referendum to decide whether the city of Vancouver is going to sell the airport, or whether it is going to proceed on its own with the construction of a $15 million air terminal. I have looked with a certain amount of jealousy and a profound amount of admiration at the excellent facilities at Dorval, and feel that it is imperative at this time that similar facilities be provided at the Vancouver international airport.
We have a rather interesting situation there in that the city of Vancouver owns approximately 475 acres of that airport, while the Department of Transport owns some 2,450 acres. The city acquired the airport some 30 years ago and to date has made capital expenditures amounting to $1,675,000, while the Department of Transport has spent $12,490,000. I emphasize these tremendous amounts of capital expenditures because there has been misleading information given to the voters in the city of Vancouver to the effect that the Vancouver international airport is a gold mine and should be retained by the city. The city of Vancouver has the advantage
Supply-Transport
of the federal government making the majority of the capital expenditures, taking care of the major part of the maintenance and, through leases from the Department of Transport, the city is able to charge landing fees and sell aviation fuel, which amounted to a revenue of some $400,000 in 1959, which was clear profit, not required to be handed over to the federal government. In 1959 it was estimated that if operating costs paid by the city and the Department of Transport were combined, the net loss in that year would have been some $850,000.
A referendum was held in 1954, in which 59.4 per cent of the voters voted to sell the airport. Approval of 60 per cent of the voters is required to effect such a sale. In December of 1960, another referendum was held in which 57.7 per cent of the voters were in favour of the sale. At present the majority of the city of Vancouver council members are in favour of selling the airport, as are the members of the board of trade and other organizations. I raise this matter at this time because another referendum is to be held on June 21, 1961. The city of Vancouver, which owns 475 acres of the property, has been unable to effect the sale to this date.
There is a proposal to establish a $13 million to $18 million jet terminal, and I am interested in this matter because it concerns the whole of the lower mainland of British Columbia as well as the city of Vancouver. I hope the citizens voting on this referendum will realize the obligations which the city must accept if the airport is not sold, and will realize the benefits which will accrue to the people of the lower mainland with the establishment of this jet terminal.
In respect of Sea island, I should like to direct the minister's attention to the fact that it is serviced from Lulu island in the mouth of the Fraser river. Present access to Sea island and the international Vancouver airport, as well as the Royal Canadian Air Force base, is by means of the Oak street bridge to Lulu island, and over the Moray channel bridge to Sea island. Some 3,000 residents live on Lulu island at the present time yet the only access to Sea island and Lulu island is by one bridge, the Moray bridge. The Eburne bridge was the responsibility of the provincial government but, due to the deterioration of this particular bridge, the provincial government decided to close it on March 13, 1961, as a result of which the Moray channel bridge, which is a two lane swinging span bridge now operated by the bridge attendants from the Eburne bridge, provides the only access to Sea island. This bridge must be opened at varying times to allow the passage of tugs and barges on the

Supply-Transport
river. I made a visit one Saturday afternoon during the last Easter recess and was fortunate, or unfortunate, depending on how one looks at the situation, in approaching the Moray channel bridge at a time when it was opened to allow tugs and barges to pass. Apparently the tugs and barges have the right of way and, although the bridge was only open for some 15 minute at that time, I counted 50 cars on my side of the bridge and 60 on the other east side waiting to go across.
I suggest this situation is of great concern because the bridge on occasion has been blocked for maintenance and repairs as long as five or six hours, as a result of which Sea island was completely isolated. This is of great concern first of all from the point of view of national defence and, second, because of the great inconvenience caused travellers going to the Vancouver international airport.
Recently a firm of consultants, John Graham Ltd., made a traffic analysis on behalf of the municipality of Richmond. I should like to list certain figures contained in this report in connection with the Vancouver international airport. The number of passengers carried in 1958 totalled 850,000; in 1960, 1,050,000. The estimates for 1965 are, 1,600,000; 1970, 2,300,000; 1975, 3,100,000; and 1980, 4,100,000.
On page 38 of the John Graham Limited report it is recorded that the volume in 1960 peak hours exceeded the practical capacity of this bridge. According to the various ministers concerned, the bridge was constructed to provide access to the federal government properties on Sea island. I would suggest that this bridge is not performing its function.
On the same page of the report there is a recommendation that a four-lane bridge should be constructed between Sea island and Vancouver. I submit that the Minister of Transport should give very serious consideration to this suggestion and I think he should also investigate my alternative suggestion of a tunnel under the Fraser river, going directly from Granville street to Sea island. I feel that it could be and should be the responsibility of the federal government to provide this necessary and much needed access to the facilities at the Vancouver international airport. In the event that the federal government becomes the owner of the international airport on June 21 the minister should give even more serious consideration at that time to the suggestion of having at least a bridge or a tunnel connecting Vancouver and Sea island. We have a precedent at the present time. The provincial government has constructed the Oak street bridge which goes on to Lulu island from Vancouver and the Deas island

tunnel which goes under the Fraser river into the Delta area. I think the minister should give this matter very serious consideration because the Vancouver area is the gateway to the east and to the Orient. It is an expanding and developing area. Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, government departments inherit the promises and often the problems of their predecessors. This department is no exception. Sometimes a candidate in his ignorance increases those responsibilities on the part of himself and his party and when he comes to Ottawa he gets a rude awakening. I had this.
The C.N.R. has failed to close a gap in northern Alberta and northern Saskatchewan in its railway line. When one looks at the map he sees it is so obvious it is an uneconomic and shortsighted way to run a railway that I took it upon myself to promise the people of my constituency that as soon as I got to Ottawa I would look into this thing and no doubt with the proper amount of pressure something could be done about it. Well, I think I have exhausted my resources in this matter. I put all the pressure possible on the department concerned. I was sent to Montreal with a mandate to interview the top brass of the C.N.R. On arrival in Montreal I got what I believe is the usual treatment a backbencher gets from the ivory tower. I would say if you can believe it that the attitude was one which no servant of the crown should offer to a sitting member, particularly if that member comes in a spirit of co-operation, looking for information rather than offering unsolicited advice on how to run a railway.
Before I was able to outline the problem from my viewpoint and ask the necessary questions it was suggested that I return to Alberta, mind my own business and forget about the whole thing. Now, this is not why I was elected. I was elected because I am rather an aggressive person and my constituents really believed that when I got down here I would do a certain amount of rational fighting. If it has to be in-fighting I can do that, too. But I took a very calm and fact-finding approach to the problem and I found out that the top brass of the C.N.R. are not imaginative. Therefore, I put it up to the department to give serious consideration to placing as top brass and top management at the head of the C.N.R. people who will at least listen to the problem when it is presented from the district concerned.
Enough of this; I want to tell the committee what the problem is. The C.N.R. has a line north of the Saskatchewan river running easterly toward Saskatchewan, and a further

railway north of the Saskatchewan river for half the province. It ends at the town called Heinsberg, about 20 miles from the Saskatchewan boundary. Between there and the Saskatchewan boundary is open parkland with no engineering difficulties. The C.N.R. railway coming up from the east ends at about the same distance from the Alberta boundary in the same type of territory. In order to take freight from Heinsberg to Winnipeg it is necessary to go through Edmonton, an extra distance of 328 miles. The same would be true for any freight going from Frenchman Butte in Saskatchewan to Edmonton. You have to go a considerable distance into Saskatchewan and double back on the main line. I am not a railroader or I would have liked to take up the challenge to run the C.N.R. myself. I was asked if I would like to do that. I declined because I am not a railroading man; I am just a backbencher.
I do not know very much about railroads, but I know you cannot haul freight 328 extra miles and be efficient or make money for the people of Canada who are paying the bills. I was told that if I could show them on paper how they could make money by building this 40 miles of railway they would build a line. Well, I cannot prove that railroads will make money today but I do think that we can cut down our deficit. I do think that by cutting out the extra haul of 328 miles you could save the taxpayers of Canada a considerable amount of money which is now going into subsidies. I am disappointed that we pay this type of top brass $75,000 because I believe that a railroad man on a considerably reduced salary could put the C.N.R. back on its feet.
One of the most important things in running any organization is morale. Today the C.N.R. is completely demoralized. I have ridden on this line some dozen times back and forth to Ottawa and from the section foreman upwards there is great discontent in the rank and file. They are concerned about the security of their jobs being threatened and they do not like working for people who have lost faith in their own railway.
I say to the minister and members of the committee through you, Mr. Chairman, we should give serious consideration next week when the bill comes up which specifically deals with the brass to putting a new chief at the head of this railway. That is what I suggest we need. When we won the battle of Alamein it was largely owing to the personal leadership of General Montgomery. When Britain won the battle of Trafalgar it was because of Nelson. I think the time is long overdue to put a man at the top of the C.N.R. who loves his railway, a man in whom the
Supply-Transport
rank and file of the railway would have complete confidence and to whom they would give natural loyalty.

Mr. Chairman, I am glad to note that the minister has returned to his seat, because I should like to deal with problems concerning the Department of Transport.
First of all, there is the problem of the Champlain bridge approaches on the north shore. Early in February, the new Montreal administration set up a committee to consider the northern approaches of Champlain bridge; the access roads to the Point St. Charles dump; a grant in lieu of a tax for Montreal harbour; the right of way for vehicles using Jacques Cartier bridge to reach St. Helen island; a proposed causeway leading to that island, as well as other problems of lesser importance.
This committee was formed of Mr. Guy Beaudet, manager of Montreal harbour and of Messrs. Lucien Saulnier, chairman of the executive committee, Lucien L'Allier, director of the public works division, Jean La-coste, director of the traffic division, and Claude Robillard, director of the town planning division.
I have always insisted on better northern approaches to Champlain bridge which is now under construction, but which should have been open to traffic early in September 1962, according to the former minister of transport.
This project, as members know, was started under a Liberal government. As things are going now-and as I said even last year- I am still of the opinion that it is a Liberal government which is going to inaugurate it. Nevertheless, I want to mention right now the approaches which, to my way of thinking, are simply awful.
At present, on the north side and according to plans, all approaches converge to the entrance of Atwater tunnel. I have said it last year and I repeat it now, Atwater tunnel has been built to replace the bridge over the Lachine canal. This tunnel is already too narrow for rush hour traffic. I do not see how it could absorb all that Champlain bridge traffic on three lanes in both directions.
I said, last year, that this was disastrous. If the department persists in refusing to build additional approaches elsewhere than through the tunnel, I should think such an attitude would be shameful.

Supply-Transport
I said before and I stated earlier today and I repeat it now-it is absolutely impossible to see how three-lane traffic to and from Champlain bridge which is now being built, can be handled by a tunnel which is already too small to absorb the rush hour traffic.
This morning, I asked the Minister of Transport a question with regard to an agreement signed yesterday between the city of Montreal and the national harbours board. I would have liked to see that document in order to know whether it deals with the matter of approaches.
A press item says:
Approaches to the Champlain bridge will, in the beginning, be at ground level.
What is the meaning of "in the beginning" and "ground level"? Does it mean that part of it will be at ground level for a few months and that, later on, some elevated lanes will be built in replacement?
All we know, is that an agreement was signed but we are not informed of its terms.
Again in the same article:
The approaches in the city of Montreal are in two sections providing access and exit to and from the bridge into existent streets mainly through Atwater tunnel.
That is what I was saying. Once again, I think it is unbelievable that people should want to throttle Atwater tunnel and bottleneck our neighbouring streets with the traffic to and from Champlain bridge. I never understood, and still fail to understand, why we should have to go down on our knees and make endless calls in order to obtain anything whenever additional federal work is to be undertaken in Montreal.
Mr. Chairman, I remember very well that when the approaches on the south shore of Victoria and Jacques Cartier bridges were built, a remarkable job was done. As a matter of fact, approaches from and to the south of those two bridges are good. And it should be pointed out that it did not cost the municipalities concerned anything except in the way of land which belonged to them.
On the other hand, in respect of approaches on the north shore, in Montreal, the federal government's attitude is entirely different. Moreover, just to prove my statement, the approaches to and from Victoria bridge on the north shore are simply atrocious. Indeed, every evening, during the rush hour, i.e. from 4.30 to 6.30, Bridge street, which leads to

Victoria bridge and Wellington tunnel from the east side are blocked. The Montreal authorities are planning to build the elevated highway at the intersection of Wellington and Bridge streets. This is a $2 million project, and I am not aware that the federal government has agreed to co-operate in any way. To build the elevated highway, the Montreal authorities will have to expropriate a whole side of Bridge street, which is a residential area, and here again, no subsidy is expected from the federal government.
Mr. Chairman, for three years now and again today, I have been deploring the approaches at the north end of Champlain bridge. As I stated a moment ago, and as I repeat now, it is a disgrace, and in view of the federal government's inaction, I call it a scandal. Can you imagine that people could decide to build a bridge costing millions of dollars, and make no provision for decent approaches?
It is like a painter who, having finished a painting, would store it in his attic for lack of a frame. We know that the frame often enhances the painting.
Again, sir, I hope that in the agreement signed with the Montreal authorities, provision has been made for approaches other than through Atwater tunnel.
On the other hand, I must recognize that this agreement includes a particular project which is very satisfactory to my constituents.
I refer to the agreement between the city of Montreal and the national harbours board for the construction of an access road to the Point St. Charles dump. This dump, which is located on the river shore in my constituency, has been a source of constant difficulties, and for 20 years every public representative has been asking that the dump be closed or that an access road be built so that trucks would not have to go through residential streets, as they do now.
I was somewhat surprised, however, that according to the latest information I received, an access road passing beneath Champlain bridge was to be built under this agreement with the federal government.
However, here is what I find in this morning's issue of Be Devoir:
The executive committee also accepted an agreement whereby an access road to the Point St. Charles dump will be built under Victoria bridge.
Has a new solution been reached? That is all for the better. I am all the happier because the article further states, and I quote:

The chairman of the committee, Mr. Lucien Saulnier, stated that thanks to this agreement, garbage trucks will have disappeared from Marguerite Bourgeois street within a month.
Now, the people who live on Marguerite Bourgeois, a residential street, have always rightly complained about the fact that trucks carrying garbage or snow, use that thoroughfare to reach the dump.
In another field, namely the construction of the east-west super-highway, there is a problem to which the city of Montreal may not be giving proper consideration.
Indeed, the municipal authorities seem to feel that the only solution is to build a subway. Well, I do not share that opinion even though I sit on the city council. We have too many surface problems to settle and we could do that much more cheaply than by building a subway.
One of the most important projects is the construction of the east-west super-highway which will pass near the river, on federal property. It seems to me that the city of Montreal and the federal government should come to an agreement for the early execution of that project.
Such a super-highway would eliminate at least part of the traffic which must go through the city, whether eastbound or westbound. It would relieve traffic on Sherbrooke, Notre Dame, Dorchester, St. James and even St. Paul and the vehicles which now go through the harbour district could use the super-highway to go east or west, thus relieving the traffic on the streets I have just mentioned.
The more so since the Montreal transportation commission could inaugurate an express bus service on that expressway, similar to the service now established on St. Denis and St. Lawrence streets, to accommodate the east-west traffic and vice versa.
I hope that we will shortly see progress in that regard. In addition, I hope that the east-west expressway will be built as soon as possible.
Turning to another matter, Mr. Chairman, I would like again to call the minister's attention to a suggestion made by the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Des-chatelets) yesterday, when he said that a lookout should be built in the vicinity of the harbour of Montreal in order that the people of Montreal may visit the place. As a matter of fact, I am sure that many Montrealers hear about the harbour but have never visited it and are not aware of what goes on there. We
Supply-Transport
are aware of its facilities and we realize its importance. It is one of the largest ports in Canada, and it must maintain its importance. Montrealers must be able to get on-the-spot information on the port. To that effect, I should like to put forward again the following suggestion made by my colleague:
Even a lookout, like those that were erected at the time of the St. Lawrence seaway development, could be set up, so that, from a height of 50 feet, people could see all the activities of Montreal.
Even if certain suggestions are made by the opposition, I hope the Minister of Transport will kindly consider them, because we often heard in the past ministers asking for suggestions to solve various problems.
I think that for the last three days the minister has been getting suggestions, both from his colleagues on the government side and from members of the opposition, and I would be glad if some of the suggestions made by members of the opposition were accepted or at least that they be given favourable consideration.
In closing, I should like to point out another suggestion made about certain problems in Montreal, and which concern the federal government. It is about the setting up of a committee or commission including members of the Montreal administration and other persons appointed by the federal government.
I said a moment ago that Mr. Beaudet and some members of the Montreal administration were members of a commission. After three or four months' sittings, recommendations were made, which, although not perfect, have none the less facilitated the settlement of three or four problems in Montreal.
Allow me, Mr. Chairman, before resuming my seat, to remind the minister that I insist on the proper development of the southern and northern approaches to Champlain bridge. I do not know the terms of the agreement, but the minister promised me this morning that he would table it in the house as soon as he received it. The tunnel can take care only of the normal traffic. It is already too small and it is no use building a six-lane roadway if the tunnel is not improved.
I am closing with this. I know you want to call it six o'clock. I am just as anxious to go home as my colleagues. Nevertheless, I am convinced that, unless the bridge approaches are improved so as to take care

Supply-Transport
of the traffic during rush hours, it will be most unfortunate. Last year I suggested the building of elevated roadways, but, whether they be elevated or underground, as long as they move the traffic to Dorchester street, I will be satisfied.
Therefore I hope the minister will give consideration to some of my suggestions and use them.

maintopic: COMMISSION OP INQUIRY, INDIAN AFFAIRS, MACKENZIE DISTRICT
COMMISSION OP INQUIRY, INDIAN AFFAIRS, MACKENZIE DISTRICT
speechtext:
1.	Has the commission of Inquiry, appointed on June 25, 1959, to Inquire generally into all matters arising out of the unfulfilled provisions of treaties 8 and 11 as they applied to Indians of the Mackenzie district, held any meetings: and, if so, upon what dates and in which places were these meetings held?
2.	Has the said commission made any report and recommendations', and if so, what are the details of the said report, and the action taken with respect to the recommendations?
Answer by: Hon. Ellen L. Fairclough (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
1.	Yes. Meetings were held from July 5 to July 17, 1959, at the following settlements:
Aklavik, Fort McPherson, Arctic Red River, Fort Good Hope, Fort Franklin, Fort Norman, Fort Wrigley, Fort Simpson, Fort Liard, Fort Providence, Hay River, Fort Resolution, Fort Rae, Snowdrift, Fort Smith.
2.	Yes. The commission recommended against the establishment of reserves in the proportions provided for in the treaties and suggested that the government open negotiations with the various Indian bands with a view to ascertaining whether in lieu of their land rights under the treaties they would be interested in monetary compensation, a combination of both, or some other form of compensation.
In connection with this general recommendation the commission made certain recommendations concerning the value of lands, mineral rights, fishing and hunting rights, establishment of Indians in settlements, welfare services, etc., all of which have been under study by an interdepartmental committee.
